title: Fig and Pip's Bunting Mystery
markdown:
When Lily drifted into slumber, whiskers twitched. Fig, a rat of remarkable cleverness, nudged his companion. “Pip, old chap. The air feels odd.” Bright eyes caught moonlight.

Pip the bunny blinked, ears flopping. “Odd? Like when my favourite carrot rolled under the sofa? Or when the milk spilled and made a funny brown puddle that looked like a sad cloud?”

“More basic than a lost root.” Fig packed his tiny satchel with dried apple and a shiny button. “The canal path seems different. The moonlight on the water usually sparkles; tonight it’s dull and muddy. And Farmer Giles’ prize-winning pumpkins are mysteriously damp, though it hasn’t rained for a week. I suspect something’s amiss.”

They slipped through the cat-flap. The familiar pine woods felt hushed, trees like watchful giants, scent thick with disturbed earth.

A light drizzle began, each droplet a soft pitter-patter on leaves.

Pip leaped onto a mossy log, fluffy tail puffing. “The deluge. We are undone. Drenched to the bone. We shall become soggy carrots. Our fur will cling like damp tea towels.”

Fig shook a drop from his whiskers. “A spot of rain hardly signals the end of our quest. The signpost should be near the old willow. Swift and sure.”

They pressed on, Pip admiring shimmering raindrops on spiderwebs — “tiny crystal chandeliers for woodland sprites” — while Fig, with quiet exasperation, urged him forward. The drizzle intensified. The path twisted unexpectedly into a small clearing bathed in silvery glow as clouds broke.

Colourful bunting fluttered between branches like festive flags.

“Look, Fig. A party. Did someone forget to invite us? Perhaps a surprise birthday for a particularly important hedgehog.”

Fig focused on the problem. The signpost leaned at a jaunty incorrect angle, now pointing toward Farmer Giles’ pumpkin patch, plump gourds looking suspiciously waterlogged.

“Aha. Precisely as I suspected. The source of the strange plant problems and the general sense of getting lost.”

“But who would move a signpost? And why is there bunting? Are we sure it isn’t a party we’re meant to crash, with tiny berry tarts and dewdrop punch?”

As they approached, a small furry figure struggled to tie a knot, paws working with frantic energy: a young badger cub, no bigger than Pip, mud on his nose, earnest concentration, unfurling another length of bunting.

He yelped, startled, dropping the bunting. “You found me. I thought I was being so quiet.”

Fig’s tone softened. “Might we inquire as to your activities? This festive array suggests a celebration, yet the signpost appears to be in distress.”

The cub wrung his paws. “My Granny Elara. She was so worried about the big rain and the wind. She said the signpost was wobbly, and if it fell into the canal it might drift away and get lost forever. Then everyone would get lost. So I moved it. Just a little. To higher ground.” He gestured sheepishly at the post, now firmly planted in soft earth. “And I thought, if it’s going to be here for a bit, it should look cheerful. Granny always says a little bit of cheer makes everything better. So I put up Granny’s party decorations.”

Pip’s mouth hung open. “You moved the signpost to save it from the rain?”

“And put up bunting for cheer?” Fig added, a rare smile spreading. Profound understanding, not a lecture: a child’s earnest if slightly misguided good deed.

The cub’s ears drooped. “I didn’t mean to make things wrong. I just wanted to help Granny, and the signpost, and everyone.”

Pip hopped forward and nudged the post gently with his nose. “It’s not wrong, little chap. It’s just very, very kind. And very pretty.”

The odd feeling, the damp pumpkins, made sense. With combined effort — Fig providing leverage, Pip offering moral support, the cub re-tying knots with newfound confidence — they carefully repositioned the signpost. The drizzle eased. A sliver of moon peeked through, casting a soft glow. The bunting, though damp, fluttered merrily.

They did not need Fig to announce that mysteries are sometimes born of a loving heart. The post stood true. The flags stayed. The path home felt familiar and right.

Dawn began to paint the east. Fig and Pip slipped back through the cat-flap, weary and content. Lily still dreaming. Two beds, two small adventurers, and somewhere by the willow a signpost wearing Granny’s bunting as if that had been the point of the canal all along.
characters: Fig (a pet rat), Pip (a pet bunny)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
